processing: Bancha leaf is deep-steamed, spread out and sun-dried for about two days, without rolling, then roasted as the last step; larger makers roast in hot sand.
harvest_season: Little is documented on the exact picking time; it uses mature bancha leaf rather than young shoots.
appearance_dry: Large, flat, whole brown leaves, with no rolling to twist them.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber-brown, as is usual for a roasted bancha.
taste_profile: Toasty and light like hojicha, with very little astringency or bitterness and a clean finish.

brewing.notes: Use a big pot, as the leaves are large, and boiling water. For several people, simmer the leaf directly in a pot of water.

vintage_note: An everyday tea sold without vintages; usually packed from the latest year's making. The roast helps it keep better than sencha, but it is still at its most fragrant within a year or so of roasting.
description:
Yoshino Nikkan Bancha is a sun-dried, roasted bancha from the Yoshino region in southern Nara, with its roots in the town of Oyodo. It is what happens when a farmhouse tea skips almost everything modern tea making does.

The big leaves are steamed hard, laid out in the sun for about two days, and then roasted. They are never rolled, so whole leaves survive to the final bag. That technically makes it a roasted green tea, a cousin of hojicha, though one with a sun-dried character of its own.

In the cup it is mild and toasty, with little bitterness and little caffeine, and it is forgiving. Boiling water and a two-minute steep work, and a big pot helps because the leaf is bulky. Simmering a handful in a kettle is perfectly traditional.

It is not rare in Japan, just less known than sencha. Look for intact leaves and a fresh, clean roast smell.
history:
This tea is said to go back to before the Edo period, though no firm date is documented.

In recent years the Oyodo Chamber of Commerce and Industry promoted it through the Yoshino Ooyodo Nikkan Bancha Project, which brought press attention and visitors and led to uses such as powdered tea in ice cream and baking.
